screenings.title: Wild Style
screenings.description: U.S., 1983 Directed by Charlie Ahearn With Lee Quiñones, Fab 5 Freddy, Lady Pink, Patti Astor Approx. 82 mins. While Lee’s masked mystery tagger ZORRO tries to get back his main flame Rose (Pink), reporter Patti Astor goes way uptown to the South Bronx to blow up the whole scene as Fab 5 Freddy tries to get rich. Joyous, raucous, explosive, premonitory, and with not one single professional actor, WILD STYLE is the movie that had Hollywood see $$$$. From ZEPHYR’s animated graf titles rivaling Saul Bass, to the epic park jam climax at the Williamsburg Bridge amphitheater with Rammellzee in a trenchcoat waving around a sawed-off, there’s scene after indelible scene: Chief Rocker Busy Bee rocking the Dixie Club while white-gloved b-boys pop and lock, the Cold Crush Brothers and the Fantastic 5 battling on the b-ball court, Grandmaster Flash on the ones and twos in his kitchen, Double Trouble freestyling on a stoop as a turtlenecked kid looks on, and graf galore—whole-cars and murals by DONDI, DAZE and CRASH and a funky-ass soundtrack by FAB and Blondie leader Chris Stein, spun throughout. Presented with support from The Roy Lichtenstein Foundation Fund

screenings.title: I Hired a Contract Killer
screenings.description: Freshly unemployed after 15 years at the same civil service post, newly turned 50, and too frightened to put himself out of his misery by his own hand, Jean-Pierre Léaud, a Frenchman living in London, decides to hire a hitman to do the dirty work for him—but this final solution runs into a wrinkle when he rediscovers his will to carry on after falling madly in love, leaving him to scramble to cancel the contract. A deadpan hilarious and disarmingly poignant comedy from Finland's eminent master of the genre, giving Léaud perhaps his finest English-speaking role.

screenings.title: Totally F***ed Up
screenings.description: The first installment in Gregg Araki’s Teen Apocalypse trilogy, Totally F***ed Up follows six queer Los Angeles teenagers who form a makeshift family as they bond through relationships, bed-hopping and societal rejection. A punk-rock mixture of Jean-Luc Godard and John Hughes films, Totally F***ed Up would go on to set a template for LGBTQ youth cinema and became one of the defining films of the New Queer Cinema movement of the 1990s.

screenings.title: The Kingdom
screenings.description: On the pale, sun soaked island of Corsica in the summer of 1995, the teenage Lesia is plucked from her sheltered life, and taken to a remote villa where her fugitive mob boss father, Pierre-Paul, is hiding out. Pierre-Paul is a menacing figure, a near stranger to Lesia, and at first she feels trapped by the secrecy and danger which defines his life. But when an assassination attempt sets a chain of bloody vendettas in motion, Lesia and Pierre-Paul are forced to go on the run together. As they flee, Lesia becomes closer than ever with her father, and as they wade together through the violent underworld which he is entrenched in, his devotion to revenge begins to rub off on her. THE KINGDOM is a story of blood: blood spilled, blood sought, and the blood which binds us.

screenings.title: Late Fame
screenings.description: CRITIC’S PICK. “A loving and lovely sensibility runs through LATE FAME, a fond and wise understanding of why some people want to become artists without making much art and why other people quit making it altogether.” – Alissa Wilkinson, The New York Times “[A] lovely and bittersweet drama... Dafoe has rarely been so tender, playing a man allowing himself to dream again for the first time in forever.” – Tim Grierson, A/V Club “Like a wonderful little poem... Samy Burch, who also wrote the astute Oscar®-nominated script for 2023’s MAY DECEMBER, has crafted another subtle but powerful work.” – Kyle Smith, The Wall Street Journal “Lyrical and enchanting... Dafoe’s performance is like a slowly unfolding wildflower.” – Owen Gleiberman, Variety “Willem Dafoe is low key and magnificent as a former poet seemingly rescued from obscurity... In a prolific career filled with complex and striking characters, the role of Ed Saxberger is a subdued but particularly rich one for Dafoe, himself a veteran of the downtown arts scene.” – Sheri Linden, The Hollywood Reporter “LATE FAME is a deliciously acidic examination of the thin line between creative aspiration and pretentious poseurdom.” – Wendy Ide, Screen International

As they abduct and interrogate suspects across Paris, the line between justice and obsession begins to blur, revealing a web of corruption and hidden truths that threatens to consume them both.

screenings.description: Nawojka, a young woman struggling with her monstrous desire, is convinced that she is struck by a strange hereditary curse and will try to escape the family shackles through Sandra, her sultry neighbor who has returned to the village.

screenings.title: The Night is Short, Walk on Girl
screenings.description: A surreal nocturnal animated odyssey from Yuasa, the mad genius behind Mind Game, rendered in a frenetic, galaxy-brained, endlessly morphing style. The Night is Short, Walk on Girl follows a mysterious high schooler known only as The Girl with Black Hair through the streets of Kyoto’s famed Ponto-Cho party district, drinking middle-aged salarymen under the table when she’s not mixing with barflies, obsessive collectors, and guerilla theater performers, all the while oblivious to the efforts of a fellow student who has been creating increasingly fantastic and contrived reasons to run into her in a gambit to win her love. A comic fable of fleeting youthful passions, as lived out through one mad, unforgettable night.

screenings.description: Brit bodybuilder Reg Park straps on the sandals and exomis to play Zeus’s swole love child in Bava’s deliciously delirious peplum, co-written by Mondo Cane’s Franco Prosperi, which follows our hulking hero—as well as Theseus and Telemachus—on a perilous mission to save Herc’s lover Princess Deianira, stricken senseless by illness, endeavoring to procure for her a sacred stone from the depths of Hades, home court of Christopher Lee’s sinister Lyco and his zombie hordes. A triumph of resourcefulness over limited resources, rich with Gothic atmosphere, swirling with nigh-psychedelic colors, and offering at every turn ample evidence of cinematographer-turned-director Bava’s consummate mastery of the motion picture apparatus.

screenings.title: 9/11, Pgm 2: the Unrecovered
screenings.description: The attacks were encoded in the national memory over seemingly endless minutes, hours, days, weeks, and months of media coverage. A quarter of a century later, it is tempting to think of 9/11 as a media event announcing material reality’s final, total subordination to the image—as Baudrillard said, “They did it. We wished it.” Yet to conceive of 9/11 in only these terms would be to overlook the lived horrors of the day and the insidious reverberations of a nationwide psychic trauma. From our historical vantage, the events of September 11 seem as fundamental to our current reality as the air we breathe. In recognition of the twenty-fifth anniversary of September 11, 2001, Spectacle presents a selection of films that confront the phenomenal and psychic impact of the attacks, and the indelible scar they left on the world. There was before, and this is after. Program 1: REICHSTAG 9/11 & DISINTEGRATION LOOP 1.1 REICHSTAG 9/11 Dir. Ken Jacobs, 2016. United States. 38 min. Silent.

screenings.title: The Cameraman
screenings.description: “Keaton at the height of his art and master of every detail of silent filmmaking.” – Rudy Blesh “A delightful piece of filmmaking within a film which is both an insight into Keaton’s own logic, and also, alas, a sort of epitaph.” – Andrew Nickolds, Time Out “Brimming with invention, ingenious set-pieces, and big laughs.” – Leonard Maltin

Figures familiar from myth—including Pegasus, the two-headed dog Dioskilos, and a memorably loathsome Medusa—share screentime with inventions original to the film, notably Andromeda’s ogrish betrothed, Calibos, and the gold-wrought mechanical owl, Bubo, in this irresistible flight of fancy, a film of “blood and thunder and lots of gory details… presented with enormous gusto and style.” [Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times]

screenings.description: Tsai’s first theatrically released film isn’t as pared down in its approach as some of his later works—it even has a rather catchy synth theme song!—but in most respects it’s pure Tsai, a film about urban loners and the city’s (largely unfulfilled) promises of connection and sexual intimacy. Lee Kang-sheng, Tsai’s acteur fétiche, stars as a teenaged Taipei arcade rat who develops an obsession with a young petty hoodlum (Chen Chao-jung) that’s a tangle of vengeful wrath and repressed lust. An extraordinary debut, in which aspects of all its maker’s films to come are visible.

screenings.title: Franz
screenings.description: Award-winning director Agnieszka Holland embarks on her most ambitious project to date, a biopic of the iconic 20th-century Czech writer Franz Kafka. Conceived as a kaleidoscopic mosaic, the film follows the imprint Kafka left on the world from his birth in 19th-century Prague to his death in post-WW1 Vienna. Franz gives audiences a brand new perspective on the life of the man behind the literary giant. In Czech and German with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Hope
screenings.description: In the remote South Korea village of Hope Harbor, police chief Bum-seok (Hwang Jung- min) and officer Sung-ae (Hoyeon) are called to find a mysterious creature that has wreaked havoc on the village. In the nearby forest, a coterie of hunters, including Sung- ki (Zo In-Sung) set out to track the beast and find themselves hunted instead. But all is not as it seems, and perceptions can be misleading. What begins as ignorance plants the seed of disaster, escalating through human conflict into a tragedy of cosmic proportions.

screenings.title: Checkout
screenings.description: This psychedelic dark comedy follows Dov, a desperate Jewish-American spy, who must convince his Israeli peers he is telling the truth about a legendary terrorist. A thirst to belong consumes his soul as he is forced to retell and remodel his adventure, all the while creating an intelligence fiasco.

screenings.title: Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty
screenings.description: A ballroom dancer returns to the studio after tragedy in this vibrant visual ode to dance.

screenings.title: La Notte
screenings.description: Novelist Giovanni Pontano (Marcello Mastroianni) is the toast of the Italian literary scene, but smothered by the trappings of success. His misery weighs heavily on his wife, Lidia (Jeanne Moreau), already carrying her own cargo of existential anguish. In the course of a day and a night—spent at a hospital sickroom, a book launch, a nightclub, and a party at an industrialist’s villa, where Giovanni flirts extensively with the host’s daughter, Valentina (Monica Vitti)—the couple must come to terms with the extinction of the love that once existed between them… or not? A film steeped in despair but thrilling in its adventurous, architectonic use of the cinematic medium, from its opening credits—an avant-jazz/musique concrète overture accompanying the industrialized Milanese cityscape—to its beguiling final scene.

screenings.title: Playtime
screenings.description: On official business in Paris, Tati’s beloved, bumbling alter-ego Monsieur Hulot discovers himself lost in a new, modern cityscape of midcentury modern glass cubes, gimcrack gadgets, squeaky pleather, and shiny chromium. A brilliant burlesque of the Bauhaus future c. 1967, using some of the most elaborate sets ever created for a French film, and an experimental narrative that has the rowdy democratic mob as its ensemble "hero."

screenings.title: Chronovisor
screenings.description: An academic’s obsession with an occult device drags her through NYC’s hidden libraries.

screenings.title: Fat Girl + Introduction
screenings.description: Twelve-year-old Anaïs is fat. Her sister, fifteen-year-old Elena, is a beauty. While the girls are on vacation with their parents, Anaïs tags along as Elena explores the dreary seaside town. Elena meets Fernando, an Italian law student; he seduces her with promises of love, and the ever watchful Anaïs bears witness to the corruption of her sister’s innocence. FAT GIRL is not only a portrayal of female adolescent sexuality and the complicated bond between siblings but also a shocking assertion by the always controversial Catherine Breillat that violent oppression exists at the core of male-female relations.

screenings.title: Totally F***ed Up
screenings.description: The first installment in Gregg Araki’s Teen Apocalypse trilogy, Totally F***ed Up follows six queer Los Angeles teenagers who form a makeshift family as they bond through relationships, bed-hopping and societal rejection. A punk-rock mixture of Jean-Luc Godard and John Hughes films, Totally F***ed Up would go on to set a template for LGBTQ youth cinema and became one of the defining films of the New Queer Cinema movement of the 1990s.

screenings.title: Boogie Nights
screenings.description: The story of a young man's adventures in the Californian pornography industry of the late 1970s and early 1980s. Cast Luis Guzmán Burt Reynolds Julianne Moore Rico Bueno John C. Reilly Nicole Ari Parker Don Cheadle Heather Graham Mark Wahlberg William H. Macy

screenings.title: Troy
screenings.description: Before The Odyssey there was The Iliad, and before Christopher Nolan’s sword-and-sandals smash there was Troy, Petersen’s rather free adaptation of Homer (with a smidge of Quintus Smyrnaeus’s Posthomerica for flavor.) Orlando Bloom’s Paris lures the lovely Helen (Dianne Kruger) away from her throne in Sparta to the city of Troy, and so launches a thousand ships from the Peloponnese hellbent on dragging her back, among those aboard the fabled warrior Achilles (Brad Pitt) and the cunning strategist Odysseus (Sean Bean), soon to test their mettle against Trojan champion Hector (Eric Bana) and his armies. A strapping slab of impassioned spectacle, opulent production design, and earnest romanticism which, though critically divisive on its initial release, has in recent months seen the ranks of its admirers swell.

screenings.title: Brazil
screenings.description: Ground into despairing dust by his routine as a low-level bureaucrat in an Orwellian near-future—drabulously conceived as a junk shop jumble by art directors Norman Garwood and Maggie Gray—Sam (Jonathan Pryce) takes flight only in his imagination, where he plays the winged savior to distressed damsel Kim Griest. A chance teleprinter error at work and a wrongful arrest, however, set Sam on a course for real adventure, one involving his dream girl’s truck-driving double, a suspected terrorist (Robert De Niro), a freakshow cocktail party, plastic surgery disasters, and much more outlandishness besides. “A melancholy, joke-ridden view of the horribleness of where we are now and the worst horribleness of where we’re heading… It’s like a stoned, slapstick 1984: a nightmare comedy in which the comedy is just an aspect of the nightmarishness.” —Pauline Kael, The New Yorker

screenings.title: Sex Is Comedy + Introduction
screenings.description: Catherine Breillat’s behind-the-scenes account of shooting Fat Girl stars Anne Parillaud as Breillat surrogate Jeanne, a director intent on getting her film’s most intimate sequence just right—even if it means alternately coaxing and battling her fragile, needy young actors (Grégoire Colin and Roxane Mesquida, virtually recreating her role from Fat Girl). Once again exploring her signature obsessions, Breillat uses this metafictional format to investigate the ethical responsibilities of the artist, the messy logistics of running a set, and the slippery nature of realism, as applied to one of filmmaking’s most challenging ordeals: the simulated sex scene. Culminating in one actor’s ribald high jinks with a body prosthetic and another’s breakthrough into shattering emotional territory, Sex Is Comedy is Breillat’s heady, brilliant synthesis of the ridiculous and the sublime.

screenings.title: Kaboom
screenings.description: A wild, witty and sex-drenched horror-comedy thriller, KABOOM tells the story of Smith (Thomas Dekker), an ambisexual 18-year-old college freshman who stumbles upon a monstrous conspiracy in a seemingly idyllic Southern California seaside town. KABOOM shares key touchstones of Araki’s early films, including scatological and absurd Valley-inflected dialogue, elements of campy gore and Araki’s troupe of arrestingly sexy guys and girls. With his sophisticated synthesis of various experiments in tone and cinematography, Araki has reached a new level of artistic maturity.

screenings.title: True Romance
screenings.description: Comic shop clerk, Elvis aficionado, and repository of cult movie esoterica, Slater’s Clarence Worley goes from nerd to knight errant after his whirlwind romance with call girl Alabama (Patricia Arquette), taking her on the lam after he forcefully retires her pimp (Gary Oldman) and finds himself holding a huge stash of contraband cocaine. A bloody valentine from screenwriter Quentin Tarantino, with a gallery of supporting players including Dennis Hopper, Brad Pitt, and Christopher Walken handling his delectable free-verse pulp poetry. Distributor: Swank Motion Pictures

screenings.title: Eve's Bayou
screenings.description: One of the essential works of the 1990s and recently selected for the Library of Congress’ National Film Registry, Eve’s Bayou is a film of rich, steamy sexuality and an incredible sense of place, that follows the loss of innocence that occurs when the daughter of a well-to-do Louisiana family (Jurnee Smollett) catches her father (Samuel L. Jackson) in a moment of infidelity. Boasting an impressive line-up of actresses, including living legends Lynne Whitfield, Debbi Morgan, Meagan Good, and Carroll, unforgettably intense as the mysterious fortune teller Elzora, it’s a seductive tour de force in an atmosphere thick with voodoo, other Creole legends, and household magic.

screenings.title: Four Adventures of Reinette and Mirabelle
screenings.description: Shot quickly in and around Paris during a production break on Rohmer’s Le Rayon Vert, this breezy, witty film traces the exploits of two young women—one an ethnology student from the city, the other an unsophisticated aspiring artist from the country. Reinette and Mirabelle (played by Joëlle Miquel and Jessica Forde) become instant friends upon meeting in the first of four vignettes that make up the film (“The Blue Hour”), and in their first two days together, they decide to become roommates in Paris. Throughout the three remaining stories, they encounter many of the inevitable characters of a modern city: the impossible waiter (“The Waiter”), the Metro-station hustler (“The Beggar, the Kleptomaniac and the Hustler”), and the snooty gallery owner (“Selling the Painting”). A Metrograph Pictures release

screenings.title: The Wedding Banquet
screenings.description: Before scaling Brokeback Mountain, Taiwanese American director Lee made this indie breakout about Wai Tung (Winston Chao, in his film debut), a gay man happily living in Manhattan with his partner who stages a sham marriage between himself and a penniless immigrant artist from mainland China in his building (May Chin) in order to please his traditionally minded parents—only to be appalled when they insist on throwing the “newlyweds” a whopper of a wedding party. A tender, emotionally grounded, sharply observed comedy of clashing cultures that’s made all the more poignant by its function as a time capsule of ’90s NYC.

screenings.title: Daughter's Daughter
screenings.description: Sylvia Chang has one of the finest roles in her formidable career in Huang’s Golden Horse Award–winning intergenerational drama, co-produced by Chang and Hou Hsiao-hsien. Chang’s Jin Aixia is the middle-aged mother of two adult daughters—one, Fan Zuer (Eugenie Liu), raised by her in Taipei, the other, Emma (Karena Lam), given up for adoption and raised in New York—who, after Fan’s tragic death, finds herself the legal guardian of the embryo that her daughter, in the midst of planning for a pregnancy via in vitro fertilization, had left behind. Tender but never maudlin, with a taste (and talent) for structural experiment, Huang’s second feature confirms the writer-director as one of the most impressive up-and-coming talents in Taiwanese cinema.

screenings.title: The Blade
screenings.description: Tsui’s masterful tribute to the martial arts films he grew up with, paying homage in particular to Chang Cheh’s 1967 wuxia landmark The One-Armed Swordsman, The Blade tells the tale of a blacksmith (Vincent Zhao) at a foundry specializing in sword manufacture who, on learning the identity of his father’s killer—tatted-up bad man Hung Yan-yan—sets out to see justice done. A dervish-like work of phantasmagoric action filmmaking that boasts rapid cutting, berserk camera movement, insanely intricate choreography, smothering closer-than-close-ups, and compositions splashed with theatrical gels. Tsui has never been anyone’s idea of a minimalist, but The Blade is what you get when he’s really firing on all cylinders: euphoric sensory overload.

Irons gives one of the most complex and moving double performances in cinema history, playing twin gynecologists who develop a truly twisted relationship with a patient. While the brothers’ bizarre surgical instruments convey a memorable dose of body horror, the true horrors of Dead Ringers are psychological in Cronenberg’s brooding and outrageous exploration of a true story. screenings.title: Se7en
screenings.description: Nearing-retirement veteran Detective Morgan Freeman and new transfer Brad Pitt track a serial killer with an advanced sense of stagecraft through a sickly, perpetually sodden city of peeling lead paint and lost souls in Fincher’s tour de force, easily one of the most stylistically influential films of the 1990s. “The look of Se7en … came out of this tight working ‘cell’ we created between David, myself, the production designer Arthur Max, and the costume designer Michael Kaplan. The four of us would meet together to discuss the art direction and visual scope of the movie, and we did several sessions like that to establish a unified plan… There was something [about Robert Frank’s photos in The Americans] that interested me, which was related to the grittiness of them, the blandness, the loneliness of a past era and the texture of death.” —Darius Khondji

screenings.title: This Long Century Presents: Salomé Lamas
screenings.description: “Working across cinema, installation, and essayistic documentary, Salomé Lamas has built a body of work that is difficult to categorize. Proposing what she calls a ‘theory-fiction,’ her films probe both the traumatically repressed and the historically invisible. From the horrors of colonial violence to the landscapes of global capital, she moves between collective memory and fiction, refusing linear narrative in favor of something more disruptive. Her latest feature, Gold and Ashes (2022–2025) traces a suffocating mother-daughter bond, while simultaneously exploring humanity’s destructive relationship to the planet. As Lamas puts it, ‘Our first object of inquiry and care should be life.’ The film fragments and refuses to settle, as Lamas constructs a dual space where power relations, mortality and spiritual consciousness collide. Existing simultaneously as a feature film, an installation, and a record/publication, Lamas shows with this latest work how she continues to push at the edges of what cinema can hold.” —Series curator Jason Evans, founder This Long Century

screenings.title: The Ninth Gate
screenings.description: Hired by a wealthy collector to authenticate a rarer-than-rare copy of Aristide Torchia’s 17th-century tome The Nine Gates of the Kingdom of Shadows, purported to allow its owner to summon the Devil, New York–based antiquarian book dealer Dean Corso (Johnny Depp) sets off for Europe—and soon finds himself contending with cutthroat cults, suspicious suicides, and a most beguiling Emmanuelle Seigner. “[Polanski] represents the essence of cinematic genius for me… [On The Ninth Gate] I learned how to appreciate the distance between the camera and the actor, and also how to move the camera—or not—at a certain point in the story. I also learned to have a strong sense of the set and its design—that the set can be an actor itself, that it can be filmed like another character in the movie. And I learned the incredible accuracy you can have when cutting from one shot to another.” —Darius Khondji

screenings.title: Crash | Sex, Death, Cars!
screenings.description: Crash is about the strange lure of the auto collision, provoking as it does the human fascination with death and the tendency to eroticize danger. Most motorists will slow down to stare at the scene of a collision they may feel their pulses quickening and become aware of the fragility of their own bodies. The characters of Crash carry this awareness a step further, cherishing and nurturing it. For them, a car collision is a sexual turn-on, and a jolting life force they come to crave.

screenings.title: A Better Tomorrow III: Love and Death in Saigon
screenings.description: Taking over the reins from John Woo, Saigon-born series producer Tsui had a homecoming of sorts with this anxiety-riddled, squib-drenched 1974-set prequel, which shows us A Better Tomorrow protagonist Mark, in his younger and more vulnerable years, running guns into war- and warlord-torn Vietnam. Chow Yun-fat slides back into Mark’s iconic duster like a second skin, Tony Leung Ka-fai enters the franchise as Mark’s cousin, brother-in-arms, and romantic foil, and Anita Mui is in fine fettle as the hardened black marketeer who melts both of their hearts. A lividly angry and downright apocalyptic ending to the trilogy, practically reeking of spent shells and fresh-spilled blood.

screenings.description: A dowdy romantic-adventure writer is hurled into a real-life adventure in the Colombian jungle in order to save her sister, who will be killed if a treasure map is not delivered to her captors. She is helped out by a brash mercenary, and together they search for the priceless gem located in the map.

screenings.title: The Warriors
screenings.description: “Waaarriors! Come out and play-ay!” Falsely accused of responsibility for the assassination of New York’s most powerful ganglord during a citywide summit in the Bronx’s Van Cortlandt Park, Swan (Michael Beck) and his fellow Warriors now have to fight their way back, block by block and mano a mano, to the safe shores of their Coney Island turf. The film’s knuckle-busting action choreography and its vision of NYC as a coliseum-like proving grounds for epic heroism—its source, at a distance, is Xenophon’s 4th century BC Anabasis—are delectable, but its greatness lies in its attention to character, how it lets us see a crew of provincial Brooklynites gradually discovering they’re the toughest dudes in town.

screenings.title: 60 Years of Jim Henson’s Time Piece
screenings.description: In 1965, Jim Henson made Time Piece, an experimental nine-minute short film that tells what he called “the story of Everyman, frustrated by the typical tasks of a typical day.” The film opens with a man—played by Henson—in a hospital bed. A doctor takes his pulse. The pulse turns into a drumbeat, which becomes the percussive soundtrack for the film, in a syncopated score created by Don Sebesky. Through a series of jump cuts, we follow the man as he walks through city streets, then suburban streets, and then the jungle. Playfully surreal sequences are bridged by short passages of stop-motion animation. As Henson described his filmmaking goals: “In Time Piece I was playing with a kind of flow of consciousness form of editing, where the image took you to another image, and there was no logic to it but your mind put it together.” While the film retains his trademark sense of humor, it is also a bold example of nonlinear editing. Time Piece played for a year at the Paris Theatre in Manhattan, along with the French art-house hit A Man and a Woman. Henson’s film was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Short Film. It remains fresh today as both a time capsule of 1960s experimental filmmaking, and as a brilliantly conceived and edited example of Henson’s creativity. Karen Falk, Archives Director of The Jim Henson Company and Vice President of The Jim Henson Legacy, will follow the screening with an in-depth look of how the film was produced, sharing materials from Jim Henson’s original production files and photography. screenings.title: The Double
screenings.description: Inspired by the Dostoyevsky novella of the same title, Ayoade’s noir-inflected sophomore feature gives a dead game Jesse Eisenberg not one but two juicy parts as both a mousy, long-overlooked office drone, Simon James, and his new colleague, the cocksure and charismatic James Simon, who no one other than Simon seems to notice is in fact Simon’s doppelgänger, and who briskly sets about invading every aspect of Simon’s life. The bleakly comic story of a man struggling to get the upper hand over himself, with Eisenberg, in his virtuoso double role, getting more than capable backup from a supporting cast that includes Mia Wasikowska, Wallace Shawn, and Cathy Moriarty.

screenings.title: Iphigenia
screenings.description: The final film of Cacoyannis’s “Greek Tragedy” trilogy, following 1962’s Electra and 1971’s The Trojan Woman, adapts Euripides’s Iphigenia in Aulis, with an exceptional Tatiana Papamoschou as the waifish, doe-eyed daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, and Kostas Kazakos and Irene Papas—the latter a throughline in the trilogy—as her royal parents, commanded to sacrifice their daughter so the Greek fleets might set sail for Helen and for Troy. Bringing a naturalistic touch to the lyric drama and grounding it in real locations, including the ruins of Mycenae and the breathtaking Peloponnese coast, Cacoyannis gives us an Iphigenia that’s faithful but not slavishly so, true to the world of antiquity yet bracingly immediate.

screenings.title: Day Night Day Night | 2006 Movies
screenings.description: A 19-year-old girl prepares to become a suicide bomber in Times Square. She speaks with a nondescript American accent, and it’s impossible to pinpoint her ethnicity. We never learn why she made her decision — she has made it already. We don’t know whom she represents, what she believes in – we only know she believes it absolutely.

screenings.title: The Muppet Show: The Very Best Episodes

screenings.title: Tokyo Melody
screenings.description: In 1984, American-born, Paris-based artist Elizabeth Lennard traveled to Japan to make a film for French television about Ryuichi Sakamoto, pop star, solo artist, film actor, and film score composer. The result, shot over the course of a frenetic week, was Tokyo Melody, a mosaic work whose structure appears to have been determined by the multi-faceted nature of its subject’s creative practice: at various points we see Sakamoto snapping photographs, cruising through Tokyo on foot or via limousine, performing onstage with Yellow Magic Orchestra, pottering around his house, and in the studio for the recording of his Illustrated Musical Encyclopedia. Made so long after his collaboration with Nagisa Ōshima on Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence, Lennard’s scintillating film, now in a new 4K restoration, captures a pivotal juncture in an extraordinary life.

screenings.title: Elevator to the Gallows (Ascenseur pour l'echafaud)
screenings.description: A self-assured businessman murders his employer, the husband of his mistress, which unintentionally provokes an ill-fated chain of events. screenings.title: Electra, My Love
screenings.description: Janscó’s radically original, downright hypnotic retelling of the Ancient Greek myth against the backdrop of the puszta, Hungary’s vast, muddy plains, is among the long-take master’s most bravura stylistic performances, its 70-minute runtime made up of only twelve intricately composed shots. Reworking the tale of Electra and her ill use at the hands of Aegisthus—the man who loved her mother and murdered her father 15 years ago—Janscó produces a timeless meditation on tyranny and rebellion—and a resounding call to resistance.

screenings.title: Paint Me a Road Out of Here + Q&A | Presented by Miss Video 4 U
screenings.description: In 1971, artist Faith Ringgold created a monumental painting “For the Women’s House” for the women incarcerated at Rikers Island jail. Fifty years later, artist Mary Enoch Elizabeth Baxter, who gave birth in prison 15 years ago, finds herself banding together with an eclectic group of activists, politicians, artists, corrections officers and Faith Ringgold herself to free the artwork with the ultimate goal of freeing the women. Paint Me a Road Out of Here is a wild tale of the painting’s whitewashed journey and the two artists who challenged the same powerful and oppressive institutions, a half century apart, with their artwork, their voices and their shared, persistent goals.

screenings.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto: Diaries
screenings.description: An extension of Omori’s short Ryuichi Sakamoto: Last Days, made in close collaboration with Sakamoto’s family, Diaries is an intimate portrait of the subject over the three and a half years following his diagnosis with terminal cancer, shown in archival footage and original material at his New York home, receiving regular chemotherapy treatments in hospital, and continuing through all trials and tribulations his creative work, with longtime friend Min Tanaka heard reading passages from Sakamoto’s journal. A film about living with a finite number of hours ahead that, remarkably, is something other than a doleful threnody; its credits roll to a 1981 song that Sakamoto wrote and performed with Yellow Magic Orchestra: “Happy End.”

screenings.title: Time and Tide
screenings.description: Back in Hong Kong after taking his shot at conquering Hollywood, Tsui returned home with both barrels blazing, producing this high-strung action melodrama about a cash-strapped expectant father (Nicholas Tse) who joins the bodyguard service of his uncle (Anthong Wong) in order to make ends meet, only to discover—along with co-worker Wu Bai—a criminal conspiracy with international implications. Triad machinations, attempted assassinations, and top-tier stunt work courtesy choreographer Hung Yan-yan make Time and Tide essential viewing for any enthusiast of go-for-broke Hong Kong action.

screenings.title: The Birds
screenings.description: Dir. Alfred Hitchcock. 1963, 119 mins. U.S. 4K DCP. With Tippi Hedren, Rod Taylor, Jessica Tandy, Veronica Cartwright. Especially experienced on the big screen, Hitchcock’s boldly music-free master class in mounting and inexplicable dread feels properly apocalyptic, a film that begins as a romcom and ends as an unending screech from the void. Tippi Hedren’s cursed Melanie Daniels (swathed in an iconic pale green coat and skirt ensemble from Edith Head) is the glamorous centerpiece to Hitchcock’s existential horror classic, her brilliantly placid performance as eerily frightening as the squawking gulls that engulf her one horrible weekend in Bodega Bay. screenings.title: Alien: Resurrection
screenings.description: The fourth entry in the Alien series brings Sigourney Weaver’s Lt. Ellen Ripley, last seen swan diving into a vat of molten steel, back from the Great Beyond—after a fashion, at least. Cloned from samples of extraterrestrial-contaminated DNA, Ripley 2.0 finds herself aboard the USM Auriga spaceship two centuries after her original’s death, and shortly thereafter contending with a new host of Xenomorphs, both fangsome foes and, now, blood relations. “Jean-Pierre… wanted to make a film that was closer to his universe, with plenty of dark humor in it… The hallways were purposely lit with green hues, which would make the actors’ skin tones come out colder… With the help of the production designer, Nigel Phelps, and the vision of Jean-Pierre, we managed in the end to make a very different kind of Alien movie.” —Darius Khondji

screenings.description: New York nightclub, The Matador, becomes the site of a high-profile murder that attracts the attention of an obsessive detective, a TV news reporter, and an elusive being living outside the realms of time and space. screenings.title: Rebels of the Neon God
screenings.description: Tsai’s first theatrically released film isn’t as pared down in its approach as some of his later works—it even has a rather catchy synth theme song!—but in most respects it’s pure Tsai, a film about urban loners and the city’s (largely unfulfilled) promises of connection and sexual intimacy. Lee Kang-sheng, Tsai’s acteur fétiche, stars as a teenaged Taipei arcade rat who develops an obsession with a young petty hoodlum (Chen Chao-jung) that’s a tangle of vengeful wrath and repressed lust. An extraordinary debut, in which aspects of all its maker’s films to come are visible.

screenings.title: Paprika
screenings.description: The fourth and final film by Kon takes place in a not-too-distant future in which therapists, using a new technology called DC Mini, are able to record the dreams of psychiatric patients. All well and good, until a raid on the lab leads to the loss of the DC Mini prototype and a bleed between the troubled subconscious images and reality, leading to a race-against-time to stop bedlam from breaking out in the streets. An admitted inspiration for Christopher Nolan’s Inception (2010), though far more visually extravagant in its vibrant, psychedelia-inflected imaginings, which climax in a thrilling, terrifying dream apocalypse burst from Kon’s fervid imagination.

screenings.title: The Little Mermaid
screenings.description: This sprightly interpretation of Hans Christian Anderson’s story was eyed by Disney as far back as the days of Snow White and the Seven Dwarves, finally surfacing in 1989. There’s a hot crustacean band, sure, but also a keening grasp of the angst, loneliness, and longing in Anderson’s tale, encapsulated in Ariel’s dream of being “Part of Your World,” a highlight of Alan Mencken and Howard Ashman's superlative songbook.

screenings.title: Goodbye, Dragon Inn
screenings.description: The Fu-Ho Grand, a movie palace in Taipei, is closing its doors. Its valedictory screening: King Hu’s 1967 wuxia epic Dragon Inn, playing to a motley smattering of spectators, including two stars of Hu’s original opus, Miao Tien and Shih Chun, watching their younger selves with tears in their eyes.

screenings.title: Romancing the Stone
screenings.description: A dowdy romantic-adventure writer is hurled into a real-life adventure in the Colombian jungle in order to save her sister, who will be killed if a treasure map is not delivered to her captors. She is helped out by a brash mercenary, and together they search for the priceless gem located in the map.

screenings.title: The Great Mouse Detective
screenings.description: Rodent supersleuth Basil and his bumbling partner must thwart evil Ratigan’s plot to depose the Mouse Queen.

screenings.title: A Better Tomorrow III: Love and Death in Saigon
screenings.description: Taking over the reins from John Woo, Saigon-born series producer Tsui had a homecoming of sorts with this anxiety-riddled, squib-drenched 1974-set prequel, which shows us A Better Tomorrow protagonist Mark, in his younger and more vulnerable years, running guns into war- and warlord-torn Vietnam. Chow Yun-fat slides back into Mark’s iconic duster like a second skin, Tony Leung Ka-fai enters the franchise as Mark’s cousin, brother-in-arms, and romantic foil, and Anita Mui is in fine fettle as the hardened black marketeer who melts both of their hearts. A lividly angry and downright apocalyptic ending to the trilogy, practically reeking of spent shells and fresh-spilled blood.

screenings.title: Pushing Hands
screenings.description: Tensions brew and language becomes a barrier when widowed tai chi master Mr. Chu (Lung Sihung) swaps Beijing for a new life in New York City, where he joins the household of his Americanized son and white daughter-in-law. Lee’s directorial debut evidences the keen eye for generational and cultural differences, as dramatized with compassion and gentle humor, that would distinguish his next two features, The Wedding Banquet (1993) and Eat Drink Man Woman (1994).

screenings.title: A. Rimbaud + Q&A

screenings.description: Before scaling Brokeback Mountain, Taiwanese American director Lee made this indie breakout about Wai Tung (Winston Chao, in his film debut), a gay man happily living in Manhattan with his partner who stages a sham marriage between himself and a penniless immigrant artist from mainland China in his building (May Chin) in order to please his traditionally minded parents—only to be appalled when they insist on throwing the “newlyweds” a whopper of a wedding party. A tender, emotionally grounded, sharply observed comedy of clashing cultures that’s made all the more poignant by its function as a time capsule of ’90s NYC.

screenings.title: Jollof Films Presents: Faat Kiné
screenings.description: “We chose Faat Kiné because the film reflects our generation more than Sembène’s previous work. Faat Kiné shows what Senegal looked like in the early 2000s through its vibrant color and comedic tone. Sembène celebrates modern African women’s economic independence while criticizing patriarchal hypocrisy and religious conservatism. The film sparks interesting discussion, and we believe our audience will have deeper thoughts about Sembène’s intentions in making this film.” —Assane Sy and Ahmad Cissé, Jollof Films

screenings.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto | Opus
screenings.description: His health failing, some six months before his death Sakamoto sat down before a Yamaha grand piano under the direction of his son, Sora, and gave a final command performance before the camera, a career-spanning 20-song set encompassing his time with Yellow Magic Orchestra (a new arrangement of “Tang Poo”), songs heard here for the first time (“BB,” a tribute to Bernardo Bertolucci), and soundtrack compositions for films (“The Last Emperor” and “The Sheltering Sky,” both for none other than “BB”), video games (“Lack of Love”), and even television commercials (“Aubade 2020”). A singularly elegiac concert film, almost hypnotic in its stripped-down simplicity.

screenings.title: Her Will Be Done + Q&A
screenings.description: Nawojka, a young woman struggling with her monstrous desire, is convinced that she is struck by a strange hereditary curse and will try to escape the family shackles through Sandra, her sultry neighbor who has returned to the village.

screenings.title: Story of Mother
screenings.description: Adapted from the enormously influential author Yu Lihua’s novel Mother and Son, Sung’s film is an enormously compassionate drama about a young mother (Li Hsiang) seen stepping out on her husband by their child, an incident that, in the wake of his long-ailing father’s death and his mother’s subsequent remarriage, feeds a fire of hatred in the boy’s heart. Depicting, with an admirable withholding of judgment and emotional acuity, new tensions arising in a rapidly modernizing society still bound by very traditional notions of feminine self-sacrifice and filial piety, Story of Mother won plaudits for its fingers-on-the-pulse contemporaneity, voted the year’s best Mandarin-language film by an association of Taiwanese critics.

screenings.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto: Coda
screenings.description: A precious glimpse into the creative process of the late synth-pop star, film composer, and activist Ryuichi Sakamoto, Schible’s deeply affecting film picks up with its introspective subject as he returns to music-making after having been diagnosed with cancer, channeling his new awareness of his mortality into his latest work.

screenings.title: Fireflies Press Presents: Morvern Callar
screenings.description: A sensory odyssey packed into an intimate story of love, death, and theft, Lynne Ramsay’s second feature stays close to its impossibly distant title character, played with a transfixing inscrutability by Samantha Morton. Passing off the work of her suicided boyfriend as her own, Morvern gets a book deal and a ticket out of gray Scotland to sunny seaside Spain for herself and her best friend (Kathleen McDermott). A film of mysterious gestures, a hieroglyph that begs to be decoded while withholding the key.

screenings.title: Fat Girl + Introduction
screenings.description: Twelve-year-old Anaïs is fat. Her sister, fifteen-year-old Elena, is a beauty. While the girls are on vacation with their parents, Anaïs tags along as Elena explores the dreary seaside town. Elena meets Fernando, an Italian law student; he seduces her with promises of love, and the ever watchful Anaïs bears witness to the corruption of her sister’s innocence. FAT GIRL is not only a portrayal of female adolescent sexuality and the complicated bond between siblings but also a shocking assertion by the always controversial Catherine Breillat that violent oppression exists at the core of male-female relations.

screenings.title: Oedipus Rex
screenings.description: Seeking source materials from which to forge a new “primal cinema,” Pasolini delved into the storehouse of mythic heritage. Taking on Sophocles’s Oedipus Rex, he begins with a prologue set in prewar Italy, and goes on to defy expectation throughout, depicting Oedipus (Franco Citti), unknowingly betrothed to biological mother Silvana Mangano, as a victim of his own ignorant innocence, here far from an unambiguously positive virtue. Pasolini’s first film in color, featuring costumes and art direction that evoke an almost science fiction vision of the ancient world, and a showy role for Carmelo Bene, then-reigning bad boy of Italian stage and screen.

screenings.description: LOST LANDSCAPES OF NEW YORK (2017-26, 83 min., HD video transferred from 35mm, 16mm and 8mm film) mixes home movies shot by New Yorkers, tourists and semi-professional cinematographers with outtakes from feature films and background “process plates” picturing granular details of New York’s cityscape. The combination of intimate moments, neighborhood memories from many New York City communities and expansive perspectives forms a 21st-century city symphony whose soundtrack will be made by the audience. Spanning much of the 20th century (1920-1980), LOST LANDSCAPES recalls buried memories of daily life, work and celebration while asking audiences to reflect on possible futures for New York City. This screening adds newly found material to the original 2017 film.

Through a chance encounter with a transfer student, he trains to become an idol, starting his search for self-identity and a journey toward greatness beyond superstardom. Written, directed, edited and entirely hand-drawn by newcomer Ryuya Suzuki over eighteen months, Jinsei (meaning “life” in Japanese) is an anime tour-de-force that announces Suzuki to the world as a bold new talent in independent animation.

screenings.description: Seeking source materials from which to forge a new “primal cinema,” Pasolini delved into the storehouse of mythic heritage. Taking on Sophocles’s Oedipus Rex, he begins with a prologue set in prewar Italy, and goes on to defy expectation throughout, depicting Oedipus (Franco Citti), unknowingly betrothed to biological mother Silvana Mangano, as a victim of his own ignorant innocence, here far from an unambiguously positive virtue. Pasolini’s first film in color, featuring costumes and art direction that evoke an almost science fiction vision of the ancient world, and a showy role for Carmelo Bene, then-reigning bad boy of Italian stage and screen.

screenings.title: RoboCop - The Director's Cut
screenings.description: I’d buy that for a dollar! For a strange few years, beginning with this runaway hit, the perverse imagination and earthy humor of Verhoeven seemed to sync up perfectly with the desires of the American multiplex-going public. In dystopian Detroit, private sector Omni Consumer Products have taken over policing and made the ultimate law enforcement machine from leftover pieces of peace officer Peter Weller—but they didn’t bank on their invention making his way up the corporate ladder of crime. A frightfully funny vision of a post-industrial cybernetic future, with Kurtwood Smith, Ronny Cox, and Muguel Ferrer an impressive trifecta of irredeemable scumbags.

screenings.title: The Misconceived | Four by James N. Kienitz Wilkins
screenings.description: A failed filmmaker turned carpenter is hired by his estranged college buddy, now a successful sculptor renovating the vacation home of his dreams.

screenings.title: Daughter's Daughter
screenings.description: Sylvia Chang has one of the finest roles in her formidable career in Huang’s Golden Horse Award–winning intergenerational drama, co-produced by Chang and Hou Hsiao-hsien. Chang’s Jin Aixia is the middle-aged mother of two adult daughters—one, Fan Zuer (Eugenie Liu), raised by her in Taipei, the other, Emma (Karena Lam), given up for adoption and raised in New York—who, after Fan’s tragic death, finds herself the legal guardian of the embryo that her daughter, in the midst of planning for a pregnancy via in vitro fertilization, had left behind. Tender but never maudlin, with a taste (and talent) for structural experiment, Huang’s second feature confirms the writer-director as one of the most impressive up-and-coming talents in Taiwanese cinema.

screenings.title: O Brother, Where Art Thou?
screenings.description: The Coens’ country-fried, Depression era, quasi-musical take on The Odyssey borrows its title—and more than a bit of its anarchic sense of humor—from Preston Sturges’s Sullivan’s Travels, choreography cues from Busby Berkeley, and rips a few dozen pages out of the Great American Songbook for good measure. Pomaded convict Everett Ulysses McGill (George Clooney) takes a powder from a Mississippi chain gang with dimwit pals John Turturro and Tim Blake Nelson in tow and sets out to scare up his Penelope (Holly Hunter), along the way running afoul of Klansmen, gangsters, sultry creek-side sirens, and a Bible-thumping Cyclops (John Goodman), even taking a quick break en route to record a jubilant rendition of “Man of Constant Sorrow.”

screenings.title: Inland Empire
screenings.description: Dir. David Lynch. 2006, 180 mins. DCP. With Laura Dern, Jeremy Irons, Harry Dean Stanton, Julia Ormond. An actress plunges into Hollywood’s seedy underbelly, attempting her comeback in a cursed production. Inland Empire was Lynch’s final theatrical feature, and his most surreal and formally audacious feature film since Eraserhead. Written scene by scene during the shooting process, it seems to spring directly from its director’s subconscious. His expressive use of crude digital-video technology lends the film an uncanny veneer of melodrama, exposing the visual lies inherent in the filmmaking art. In a 2006 interview with Reverse Shot, Lynch extolled the virtues of the new: “I’m totally embracing the digital world in sound and picture, and I just can’t believe how much control and how many tools are available to us. It’s really beautiful.” Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Bird in Hand + Q&A
screenings.description: Inspired by Roscher’s own biracial experience, BIRD IN HAND follows the newly engaged Bird Rowe (Alisha Wainwright) as she returns to her rural hometown to plan the wedding with her narcissistic hippie mother Carlotta (Christine Lahti). Bird also has a hidden agenda, one that leads her to her mother’s new neighbors, a misguided couple on a mission to ‘rebrand’ a plantation. Truth, lies, and fantasy collide against that backdrop, leading to a surprising climax as tender as it is funny.

screenings.title: Midnight in Paris
screenings.description: Screenwriter, would-be novelist, and romantic-at-heart Owen Wilson, on vacation in the City of Lights with level-headed fiancée Rachel McAdams, sets out on his own one night after a wine tasting and finds himself suddenly in the Jazz Age Paris of Fitzgerald and Hemingway, Dali and Picasso—an invigorating draught of bohemian freedom that sets our protagonist to seriously interrogating his life choices. “We talked about pushing the color even more in the period scenes, in order to distinguish them from the present-day ones. The Paris of today would be normal and generic, bland and desaturated, and when you entered the Paris of the 1920s the colors would be more warm, lush and flamboyant, with lots of brown and gold and red.” —Darius Khondji

screenings.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto: Coda
screenings.description: A precious glimpse into the creative process of the late synth-pop star, film composer, and activist Ryuichi Sakamoto, Schible’s deeply affecting film picks up with its introspective subject as he returns to music-making after having been diagnosed with cancer, channeling his new awareness of his mortality into his latest work.

screenings.title: The Plagiarists | Four by James N. Kienitz Wilkins
screenings.description: When a young white couple’s car breaks down after a weekend getaway, they’re helped by an older black man who inspires them with his creative wisdom. When they discover six months later that the words he spoke might not be his own, they’re horrified, fixating on his “crime” while forced to confront the originality of their own lives.

screenings.title: Train to Busan
screenings.description: Divorced, depressed, and brutally overworked, hedge fund manager Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) has hardly any time to devote to his young daughter, Su-an (Kim Su-an), so the birthday trip they’re taking together—a 280-mile train ride from Seoul to Busan, where they’re going to meet with her mother—is a very, very big deal. Life or death, in fact, because while en route a zombie apocalypse breaks out across Korea and on the speeding train itself, leaving Seok-woo, Su-an, and a dwindling handful of uninfected passengers to fight for their lives all the way to their final destination… if it’s still there. Jang’s score, mixing electronic and orchestral elements, moving freely from mournful to menacing, and contributing immeasurably to the film’s mounting momentum, is among his very finest.

screenings.title: Alien: Resurrection
screenings.description: The fourth entry in the Alien series brings Sigourney Weaver’s Lt. Ellen Ripley, last seen swan diving into a vat of molten steel, back from the Great Beyond—after a fashion, at least. Cloned from samples of extraterrestrial-contaminated DNA, Ripley 2.0 finds herself aboard the USM Auriga spaceship two centuries after her original’s death, and shortly thereafter contending with a new host of Xenomorphs, both fangsome foes and, now, blood relations. “Jean-Pierre… wanted to make a film that was closer to his universe, with plenty of dark humor in it… The hallways were purposely lit with green hues, which would make the actors’ skin tones come out colder… With the help of the production designer, Nigel Phelps, and the vision of Jean-Pierre, we managed in the end to make a very different kind of Alien movie.” —Darius Khondji

screenings.title: Pushing Hands
screenings.description: Tensions brew and language becomes a barrier when widowed tai chi master Mr. Chu (Lung Sihung) swaps Beijing for a new life in New York City, where he joins the household of his Americanized son and white daughter-in-law. Lee’s directorial debut evidences the keen eye for generational and cultural differences, as dramatized with compassion and gentle humor, that would distinguish his next two features, The Wedding Banquet (1993) and Eat Drink Man Woman (1994).

screenings.title: The Creature from the Black Lagoon in 3-D
screenings.description: Dir. Jack Arnold. 1954, 79 mins. Restored 3-D DCP. With Richard Carlson, Julie Adams, Richard Denning. In this classic Universal Pictures monster movie, scientists drug and ensare “the creature,” who becomes enamored with head scientist David Reed’s (Richard Carlson) female assistant, Kay (Julie Adams) while in captivity. When the lonely creature, “a living amphibious missing link,” escapes from detainment, he kidnaps the object of his affection, setting into motion a rescue mission, as well as a campaign to cast the ominous creature back to the depths from whence he came. Beloved for its brilliantly designed monster, as well as for its trailblazing use of 3-D, Creature from the Black Lagoon remains a touchstone of Hollywood horror, influencing Guillermo del Toro’s The Shape of Water. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: The Taking of Pelham One Two Three
screenings.description: Lower East Side native Walter Matthau wears perhaps the broadest tie in film history as a grousing Transit Authority lieutenant who gets an unlikely shot at heroism when a group of criminals take a downtown 6 train hostage and demand a million dollars from the flat-broke city. Engineered with perfect pace and verve by the underrated Sargent, with growly, jowly Matthau at his hangdog best.

screenings.title: Carnival of Souls
screenings.description: Dir. Herk Harvey. 1962, 78 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Candace Hilligloss, Sidney Berger, Frances Feist. One of the greatest low-budget American creepshows ever made, this maximally eerie trip into the surreal has proven wildly influential—and unforgettable to anyone who has surrendered to its peculiar powers. Hilligloss plays a woman who descends into a twilight netherworld after surviving a car accident in her tiny Kansas town. Haunted by the image of a nightmarish specter pursuing her, she begins to question her sanity. Memorably shot around the midwestern environs of wide-open stretches of land and abandoned amusement parks, this B-movie cult classic is a macabre masterpiece that always makes it feel like it’s 3 a.m., no matter what time you watch it. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Still Film + Q&A | Four by James N. Kienitz Wilkins
screenings.description: In Still Film, his imaginative, incisive ode to movie culture and its beguiling hold on our imagination, Brooklyn-based artist-filmmaker James N. Kienitz Wilkins takes four decades of moving-image circulation to task. The film’s narration, modeled on an actual legal deposition, accompanies a procession of 35mm publicity stills culled by Wilkins from studio press kits. As the film runs through its carousel of Hollywood imagery of yesteryear, the courtroom characters—all performed by Wilkins himself, in his characteristically gravelly, rapid-fire voice—address the shapeshifting nature and mythologizing power of the moviegoing experience. Swirling around unverified facts and conspiracy theories while touching on the technological obsolescence and arcane obsessions that fuel true cinephila today, Wilkins’s playful, subjective journey interrogates the subject of truth itself.

screenings.title: Medea (1969)
screenings.description: Returning to the well of Greek myth, Pasolini fixed on the figure of Medea, the pagan priestess loved and left behind by the questing Jason, whose story became for Pasolini a symbol of the colonization of the classical world and the vanquishing of the precious forces of the irrational. Opera star Maria Callas, not singing and barely speaking in her only dramatic role, is riveting in her interpretation of the Medea of Euripides’s tragedy, a woman manipulated by a power-hungry adventurer, driven to vengeance by deceit.

screenings.title: The Misconceived | Four by James N. Kienitz Wilkins
screenings.description: A failed filmmaker turned carpenter is hired by his estranged college buddy, now a successful sculptor renovating the vacation home of his dreams.

screenings.title: Electra, My Love
screenings.description: Janscó’s radically original, downright hypnotic retelling of the Ancient Greek myth against the backdrop of the puszta, Hungary’s vast, muddy plains, is among the long-take master’s most bravura stylistic performances, its 70-minute runtime made up of only twelve intricately composed shots. Reworking the tale of Electra and her ill use at the hands of Aegisthus—the man who loved her mother and murdered her father 15 years ago—Janscó produces a timeless meditation on tyranny and rebellion—and a resounding call to resistance.

screenings.title: Kaboom
screenings.description: A wild, witty and sex-drenched horror-comedy thriller, KABOOM tells the story of Smith (Thomas Dekker), an ambisexual 18-year-old college freshman who stumbles upon a monstrous conspiracy in a seemingly idyllic Southern California seaside town. KABOOM shares key touchstones of Araki’s early films, including scatological and absurd Valley-inflected dialogue, elements of campy gore and Araki’s troupe of arrestingly sexy guys and girls. With his sophisticated synthesis of various experiments in tone and cinematography, Araki has reached a new level of artistic maturity.

screenings.title: Train to Busan
screenings.description: Divorced, depressed, and brutally overworked, hedge fund manager Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) has hardly any time to devote to his young daughter, Su-an (Kim Su-an), so the birthday trip they’re taking together—a 280-mile train ride from Seoul to Busan, where they’re going to meet with her mother—is a very, very big deal. Life or death, in fact, because while en route a zombie apocalypse breaks out across Korea and on the speeding train itself, leaving Seok-woo, Su-an, and a dwindling handful of uninfected passengers to fight for their lives all the way to their final destination… if it’s still there. Jang’s score, mixing electronic and orchestral elements, moving freely from mournful to menacing, and contributing immeasurably to the film’s mounting momentum, is among his very finest.

screenings.title: Heathers
screenings.description: “Dear Diary: My teen-angst bullshit now has a body count.” A caustic rejoinder to John Hughes’s ’80s Brat Pack pictures, Lehmann’s savage suburban satire brought out the sociopathic side of Christian Slater’s too-cool outlaw persona, casting him as J.D., the motorcycle-riding new arrival at Ohio’s Westerburg High School who recruits Winona Ryder’s at-first pliable Veronica Chandler into his increasingly unhinged plans to humble their class’s ruling clique of three terrible popular girls named Heather. Clearly having a ball with Daniel Waters’s imminently quotable, coal-black screenplay, Ryder gives more than a few line-readings for the ages here; just try to keep “What’s your damage?” out of your vocabulary after viewing.

screenings.title: The Double
screenings.description: Inspired by the Dostoyevsky novella of the same title, Ayoade’s noir-inflected sophomore feature gives a dead game Jesse Eisenberg not one but two juicy parts as both a mousy, long-overlooked office drone, Simon James, and his new colleague, the cocksure and charismatic James Simon, who no one other than Simon seems to notice is in fact Simon’s doppelgänger, and who briskly sets about invading every aspect of Simon’s life. The bleakly comic story of a man struggling to get the upper hand over himself, with Eisenberg, in his virtuoso double role, getting more than capable backup from a supporting cast that includes Mia Wasikowska, Wallace Shawn, and Cathy Moriarty.

screenings.title: Small Change
screenings.description: From first kisses to more sinister secrets, all of the loneliness and wonderment and danger and astonishing endurance that distinguish the years we pass between infancy and adolescence are contained here in Truffaut’s string of loosely connected vignettes concerning a group of schoolchildren living in the provincial town of Thiers in central France and their very involved instructor (Jean-François Stévenin). A film brimming with pleasures for children and adults both, unmistakably sweet-spirited while refreshingly free of sentimental treacle. “A comedy, a romance, a mystery—in a word: childhood—captured, distilled, and transformed effortlessly from sketchbook to symphony in the hands of a master.” —Wes Anderson

screenings.title: High and Low
screenings.description: Kurosawa’s formal genius and rare humanism are on full display in this white-knuckle thriller—source of an upcoming remake by Spike Lee—which transposes the materials of an Ed McBain novel to contemporary Japan, starring Toshiro Mifune as a rich industrialist thrown into a nerve-shredding situation after, first believing his son has been kidnapped, discovering that his chauffeur’s child was taken by accident. Boasting nigh-constant visual invention, geometric precision of framing, an inventive narrative structure, and a bevy of staggering set pieces—the train hand-off! the down-and-dirty G.I. bar!—High & Low is a virtuoso work that’s also a deeply moral one, exploring the meaning of “justice” in a society defined by vast economic disparity.

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
screenings.description: Dir. William Greaves, David Greaves. 2026, 100 mins. U.S. DCP. This breathtaking miracle of a movie is the finally realized, posthumous passion project of legendary filmmaker William Greaves, an intimate chronicle of the people, culture, and meaning of the Harlem Renaissance of the early 20th century. In 1972, Greaves—best known today as the director of the beloved meta-documentary Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One and director-producer of the groundbreaking TV program Black Journal—threw a party in Duke Ellington’s apartment, gathering an extraordinary group of artists, writers, poets, actors, musicians, and thinkers who were part of that singularly fecund period of American history. With loose-limbed camerawork that captures such hallowed figures as Richard Bruce Nugent, Aaron Douglas, Arna Bontemps, James Van Der Zee, and other legends in astonishingly beautiful color footage, Greaves created a living, breathing, one-of-a-kind document never seen by audiences in Greaves’s lifetime, but now completed by the filmmaker’s son, David Greaves. Once Upon a Time in Harlem is at once a portrait of a community of the 1920s and the changing sociopolitical tides of the 1970s, and a centenary celebration of the highest order. A NEON release. Tickets: $35 / discounted for MoMI and NYFF members ($30). There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.description: Inspired by Roscher’s own biracial experience, BIRD IN HAND follows the newly engaged Bird Rowe (Alisha Wainwright) as she returns to her rural hometown to plan the wedding with her narcissistic hippie mother Carlotta (Christine Lahti). Bird also has a hidden agenda, one that leads her to her mother’s new neighbors, a misguided couple on a mission to ‘rebrand’ a plantation. Truth, lies, and fantasy collide against that backdrop, leading to a surprising climax as tender as it is funny.

screenings.title: The Practice of Love
screenings.description: Export’s third feature is a feminist upending of film noir conceits starring Adelheid Arndt as a journalist who uncovers a murderous conspiracy that, upon further investigation, may very well have a connection to her unhappy personal life. “An anti-romance in which the heroine, oscillating between two relationships, gradually discovers that both are impossible, not because the subjective processes of ‘love’ are defective, but because the objective, social matrix in which both her male lovers operate is corrupt, immoral, murderous: in this film, the male world and its power structures cancel the possibility of love beyond the matter of sexuality, that is the objectification of love. Export makes use of techniques drawn from her earlier experimental cinema, video and conceptual photography to expand the possibilities of narrative feature filmmaking and to disintegrate some of its overdetermined conventions.” —Gary Indiana

screenings.title: Rose
screenings.description: Dir. Markus Schleinzer. 2026, 94 mins. Austria/Germany. DCP. German with English subtitles. In this enthralling fable of faith and social intolerance, the protean Sandra Hüller fully inhabits the daunting role of a 17th-century woman who has disguised herself as a male soldier in the Thirty Years’ War, only to continue the ruse after battle as she reintegrates into society. Though at first she is welcomed into the secluded, woodsy Protestant community, where she is able to own property, marry, and father a child, Rose increasingly draws suspicion from the locals as rumors about her arise. Shot in austere black-and-white, this meticulously detailed historical drama about a woman’s drive toward self-empowerment elegantly dramatizes the two-sided coin of human nature—the striving for personal freedom we all crave and the narrow-minded bigotry that stands in our way. Hüller won the Silver Bear for Best Leading Performance at the 2026 Berlin International Film Festival. A MUBI release. Tickets: $35 / discounted for MoMI and NYFF members ($30). There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Nostos: The Return
screenings.description: Rather than weighing the merits of one translation of The Odyssey against those of another, Piavoli dispenses with language—or, at least, readily comprehensible language—altogether, giving us an interpretation of the Homeric epic that is first and foremost a sensual, audiovisual experience, what dialogue there is spoken in a hotchpotch of ancient Thessalonian Greek, Sanskrit, and Latin. Free of the anxiety of influence, Piavoli—in his first foray into fiction filmmaking in a career that stretches back to the 1950s—transforms his source into a lyric memory piece, difficult to describe, impossible to forget, and at times positively overwhelming in its beauty.

screenings.title: Valie Export Shorts Program
screenings.description: A provocative program of short films by Export whose work, focused in her words, on “the body and moreover the female body,” can be viewed as both parallel to and a response against that of the male-dominated Viennese Actionists. Featuring the confrontational and mock-erotic Self-Portrait with Head; Touch Cinema, a document of Export’s taboo-busting performance piece; Man & Woman & Animal, an “assertion and affirmation of female sexuality and its independence from male values and pleasures” [Joanna Kierman]; Syntagma, a frenzied study of the fragmented female form; and Lust, per the director “a continuation of my previous work with the body as a vehicle for social codes.

screenings.title: Common Carrier | Four by James N. Kienitz Wilkins
screenings.description: A collection of vignettes and conversations with various full-time and part-time artists, several featuring Wilkins himself, the kaleidoscopic Common Carrier’s images are almost entirely “overlapped,” as are its dialogues, which among other things address schizophrenia, mystical “aura,” division of labor, and constitutional law, these varied discussions sharing the soundtrack with disparate radio feeds from WNYC and Hot 97 that are united by the recurrence of the word “work.” A rich and ruminative film about making do in the 21st century, eking out a creative existence in the scant free time that’s left over after the other obligations have been met.

screenings.title: Concessions + Q&A
screenings.description: Q&A with Writer/Director Mas Bouzidi and actors Josh Hamilton, Rob Riordan, Jonathan Lorenzo Price, and Lana Rockwell following the 10/4 screening of Bouzidi's debut feature, Concessions (2025). The discussion will be moderated by Charlotte Wells (director of Aftersun).

screenings.title: Wings of Desire
screenings.description: In Wim Wenders’ iconic Wings of Desire, two angels, Damiel and Cassiel, glide through the streets of a divided Berlin, observing the bustling population. When Damiel falls in love with lonely trapeze artist Marion, the angel longs to experience life in the physical world. Featuring a showstopping performance by a young Nick Cave, crooning the title track from From Her to Eternity, Wings of Desire is one of the most inexhaustible modern films.

screenings.title: The Silence of the Sea with Hail, Sarajevo
Chronovisor
screenings.description: While writing a monograph on historical theories of memory, Béatrice (Anne Laure Sellier), a respected academic, becomes beguiled by the allegedly true story of the Chronovisor, an occult device said to reproduce visuals from any point in history on a TV screen. Her obsession with the mysterious machine drags her from her Upper East Side apartment through the depths of New York City’s hidden libraries, to the edge of a breakthrough.

screenings.title: The Silence of the Sea with Hail, Sarajevo
Cinema Tehran Presents: Chicken with Plums
screenings.description: Tehran, 1958. After his beloved violin is broken, renowned musician Nasser Ali Khan loses his desire to live. Confined to bed, he drifts through memories and dreams of his youth, his family, and the great lost love that inspired his music…

screenings.title: On a String + Q&A
screenings.description: Isabel (Isabel Hagen) is a young, Juilliard-trained violist still living at home with her parents in the heart of New York City. She’s trying to make a living playing gigs with her friends but when her toxic ex- boyfriend reappears, who also happens to be the Philharmonic’s “newest, hottest cellist,” he informs her of a viola opening in the prestigious orchestra. Nothing can go wrong, right?

screenings.title: The Sun Never Sets
screenings.description: Free-spirited Wendy (Dakota Fanning) is at a crossroads in her relationship with older divorced dad Jack (Jake Johnson, New Girl) that is only further complicated when an old flame (Cory Michael Smith, Sentimental Value) re-enters her life. Set in perpetually sunny summertime Anchorage and featuring a career-best performance by Fanning, THE SUN NEVER SETS is a funny and endearing return to form for mumblecore auteur Joe Swanberg.
