screenings.title: Tender Loving Care
screenings.description: Dir. Mike Leigh. 2026, 107 mins. U.K. DCP. One of our most steadfast, unflinching chroniclers of the human condition, Mike Leigh has now crafted, along with a customarily brilliant ensemble, a portrayal of overwhelmed, resilient lives in post-Brexit England that should be received as one of his signature works. At its center is Amy (Kate O’Flynn), a government child protection worker who, after a failed relationship, has moved back in with her chipper best friend, Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson), whose job as a social services officer is a daily confrontation with anger and resentment. Meanwhile, Amy’s aging parents (Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson), concerned with their daughter’s happiness, suddenly have to contend with a crisis of their own. Smiling through their struggles—with or without a trusty bottle of wine—these finely drawn characters, and all of the remarkable supporting characters with whom they come into contact, speak volumes about the U.K.’s underfunded and fragmented care sector. Avoiding didacticism and maintaining a leveling sense of humor, Leigh shows, with clear-eyed compassion, the difficulty of asking for—and accepting—help in a world that continually lets us down. A Bleecker Street release. Tickets: $35 / discounted for MoMI and NYFF members ($30). There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: All the Mornings of the World + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: An ambitious young musician’s life becomes entwined with that of his reclusive master in director Alain Corneau’s haunting portrait of composer Marin Marais and his teacher, Monsieur de Sainte-Colombe. With a landmark score by Jordi Savall–whose viola da gamba recordings inspired novelist Pascal Quignard’s original story–Tous les Matins du Monde is a transporting meditation on artistic devotion, memory, and longing.

screenings.title: Bitter Christmas
screenings.description: Dir. Pedro Almodóvar. 2026, 111 mins. Spain. DCP. Spanish with English subtitles. The incomparable Almodóvar has been rendering the life of the creative mind on screen for five decades, with exquisite attention to every nuance of both aesthetic design and human emotion. With his complexly conceived latest, he uses a metacinematic framework to explore the artist’s tenuous relationship between fiction and reality. The sublimely expressive Bárbara Lennie stars as Elsa, a well-known actress suffering from debilitating migraines whose directorial efforts had failed upon release but have become cult classics. While trying to maintain a relationship with her loyal boyfriend Bonifacio (Patrick Criado), a fireman moonlighting as a stripper, she becomes inspired by the travails of her friends to write a new script. Yet Elsa’s story is itself a story—being written by Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia), an Almodóvar-esque filmmaker who is, in turn, taking his cues from the lives of those around him. Mixing the irreverence of early Almodóvar with the somber melodrama of his later work, Bitter Christmas insightfully details the vampiric nature of artistic creation and how we use fiction to try and right the wrongs of our lives. A Sony Pictures Classics release. Tickets: $35 / discounted for MoMI and NYFF members ($30). There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Wings of Desire
screenings.description: In Wim Wenders’ iconic Wings of Desire, two angels, Damiel and Cassiel, glide through the streets of a divided Berlin, observing the bustling population. When Damiel falls in love with lonely trapeze artist Marion, the angel longs to experience life in the physical world. Featuring a showstopping performance by a young Nick Cave, crooning the title track from From Her to Eternity, Wings of Desire is one of the most inexhaustible modern films.
screenings.country: Wings of Desire Drama, Fantasy, Romance

screenings.title: The Taking of Pelham One Two Three
screenings.description: Lower East Side native Walter Matthau wears perhaps the broadest tie in film history as a grousing Transit Authority lieutenant who gets an unlikely shot at heroism when a group of criminals take a downtown 6 train hostage and demand a million dollars from the flat-broke city. Engineered with perfect pace and verve by the underrated Sargent, with growly, jowly Matthau at his hangdog best.

screenings.title: The Terminator
screenings.description: Too many sequels and an incalculable cultural impact later, it’s sometimes forgotten what a hot and nasty little movie Cameron’s original Terminator was, dropping peak-physique Schwarzenegger into a sleazy Los Angeles of leather bars, punk rockers, and skid rows, where he quickly proceeds to killing cops by the score and tracking down mother-to-be of humankind’s savior Linda Hamilton. Working for the very last time with budget constraints, Cameron—and FX gurus Stan Winston and Gene Warren Jr.—deliver the goods and how, in a grimy lil’ chef d’oeuvre that gave us Cyberdine, Skynet, and a whole lexicon for discussing extinction-level singularity events.

screenings.description: One breathtaking composition follows another in Scorsese’s adaptation of Edith Wharton’s Pulitzer Prize–winning masterpiece about social mores (and taboos) amongst New York’s viperous moneyed classes in late 19th-century New York, brought to life by an all-star lineup of craftspeople including cinematographer Michael Ballhaus, editor Thelma Schoonmaker, production designer Dante Ferretti, and composer Elmer Bernstein. It was, Ryder stated during a recent appearance on (of all things) Hot Ones, “The role of a lifetime.”

screenings.title: Socrates
screenings.description: Beginning in the mid-’60s and ending with his death in 1977, Rossellini committed himself to producing a series of films, telefilms, and serial works that would together constitute a narrative of human progress and the history of ideas from aleolithic to present times. Socrates, initiating a tetralogy of works on epoch-defining thinkers, sets its scene in an Athens humbled by Sparta and increasingly irritated by the prickly, prodding philosopher in their midst, finally determined to silence him. Using out-of-vogue in-camera effects to transform an ancient Spanish village into Athens, probing scenes with his customized, remote-controlled Pancinor zoom, and employing a dirge-like electronic score by Mario Nascimbene, Rossellini gives us a singular vision of antiquity, one that’s downright avant-garde.

screenings.title: Behemoth!
screenings.description: Dir. Tony Gilroy. 2026, 124 mins. U.S. DCP. Pedro Pascal gives the performance of his career so far as Alex, a cellist picking up the pieces of a fractured life, in this American drama of uncommon intelligence, humor, and grace from Academy Award–nominated writer-director Tony Gilroy (Michael Clayton). A former child prodigy living in the shadow of a storied musical family, Alex has left his position with an orchestra in Chicago—fleeing a soured relationship with a manic ex (Olivia Wilde)—and returned to Los Angeles to record Hollywood film scores and resolve unfinished family business. Using a deft flashback structure to weave in and out of his adult life, while cleverly employing a panoply of original movie compositions to both accompany and comment upon them (in a soundtrack featuring nine of the industry’s leading musicians), Gilroy turns Alex’s desire for stability, meaning, and redemption into a sophisticated drama of the highest order. Behemoth! is a thundering, savvy tribute to the power of music that builds to an emotional wallop of a climax, also featuring stellar supporting work from Eva Victor, Alexa Swinton, Kaya Ralls, Erik Griffin, JoBeth Williams, and Margarita Levieva, with Hank Azaria and Will Arnett. A Searchlight Pictures release. Tickets: $40 / discounted for MoMI and NYFF members ($30). There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. screenings.title: An Autumn's Tale
screenings.description: Newly arrived in New York City from Hong Kong and unhappily reunited with boyfriend Danny Chan, Jennifer (Cherie Chung) finds a guide to this strange new world in the person of distant relation Samuel Pang, aka “Sampan” (Chow Yun-fat, at his most goofily charming)… and the prospect, possibly, of something more. A time capsule of ’80s NYC—particularly Chinatown—and a perfectly delightful blend of odd-couple romance and amiable comedy from Cheung and longtime collaborator Alex Law, who took home Best Screenplay honors at the 7th Hong Kong Film Awards for his work here. (Lowell Lo’s heartstring-tugging score was, alas, robbed.)

screenings.title: Bread Day preceded by The Train Stop
screenings.description: “In Loznitsa’s The Train Stop, in the middle of the night, the train doesn’t arrive. The waiting room is full of heavy sleepers, some folded over on their laps, some splayed out over the benches. What could rouse them? Maybe the answer is not a train, but a film. Consider Dvortsevoy’s similarly existential Bread Day. Sure, the rickety cart carrying the week’s delivery of bread to Township 3 of Zhikharevo barely seems to count as a train. It’s manually pushed by the pensioners who will soon argue strenuously with each other as they divvy up its contents. But their shouting is so vigorous, their insults so inventive, that questions of categorization quickly dissipate as the elderly residents, their goats in tow, battle to have the last word.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.title: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
screenings.description: Dir. Noah Segan. 2026, 88 mins. U.S. DCP. In a star turn of effortless command and charisma, John Turturro plays Harry, an aging petty thief from the Bronx who knows his professional days are numbered: the tactile craft of the pickpocket has become increasingly irrelevant in a digital world. Yet he must still make ends meet, especially in caring for his severely disabled wife. When Harry swipes the wallet of an ill-chosen mark (Will Price), however, he is thrust into a borough-hopping race against time to put things back in their right place. Building to a poignant climax, writer-director Noah Segan’s elegant love letter to both New York and to bygone cinematic eras recalls both the 1970s, with its grungy urban antiheroes, and the 1990s, in its American indie ethos. In addition to being a peak of Turturro’s illustrious career, the film features a terrific cast including Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, Tatiana Maslany, Victoria Moroles, and Kelvin Han Yee. A Sony Pictures Classics release. Tickets: $35 / discounted for MoMI and NYFF members ($30). There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Mermaids
screenings.description: It’s 1963, and different-drummer single mother Cher has decided to move from Oklahoma to smalltown Massachusetts, uprooting her two daughters, nine-year-old Kate and Catholicism-obsessed 15-year-old Rachel (Winona Ryder, who provides the narration). What follows includes JFK assassination trauma, a pregnancy scare, mother-daughter sexual competition, and one miraculous rescue, with devastating dynamic duo Cher and Ryder pushing one another to histrionic heights.

screenings.title: RoboCop - The Director's Cut
screenings.description: I’d buy that for a dollar! For a strange few years, beginning with this runaway hit, the perverse imagination and earthy humor of Verhoeven seemed to sync up perfectly with the desires of the American multiplex-going public. In dystopian Detroit, private sector Omni Consumer Products have taken over policing and made the ultimate law enforcement machine from leftover pieces of peace officer Peter Weller—but they didn’t bank on their invention making his way up the corporate ladder of crime. A frightfully funny vision of a post-industrial cybernetic future, with Kurtwood Smith, Ronny Cox, and Muguel Ferrer an impressive trifecta of irredeemable scumbags.

screenings.title: Brief Encounter
screenings.description: Lean’s simple, tender, and terribly emotionally direct film, featuring never-better Noël Coward dialogue and a Rachmaninoff theme that grows insuperably sad with repetition, follows an affair between a middle-class couple (Celia Johnson and Trevor Howard) who happen to be inconveniently married to other people, their mutual love and mutual agony increasing over the course of seven meetings and departures that begin with a chance in a railway station buffet. One of the great screen romances, full stop.

screenings.title: The Adventures of Prince Achmed: 100th anniversary screening with live musical accompaniment
screenings.description: Introduced by Whitney Grace, author of Lotte Reiniger: Pioneer of Film Animation Dir. Lotte Reiniger. 1926, 80 mins. Germany. 35mm. Eleven years before Disney’s Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, Lotte Reiniger’s stop-motion feature The Adventures of Prince Achmed, debuted in 1926 at the Volksbühne in Berlin, during the height of the Weimar Republic. Adapted from the tales known as the Arabian Nights, the film follows the adventures of a young prince atop a magical, flying horse who joins forces with the likes of Aladdin and a fabled witch. To evade his destined ill fate, he saves a beautiful princess and battles a sorcerer’s army of monsters. This thrilling, sensuous tale, told through Reiniger’s meticulous cut-paper silhouette animation technique, still enthralls audiences of all ages one hundred years later. Featuring live musical accompaniment by Charlie Judkins and preceded by a lecture by Whitney Grace, author of Lotte Reiniger: Pioneer of Film Animation. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission. Guest speaker Whitney Grace is a professional writer, researcher, appraiser, and pop culture historian. Her books include Lotte Reiniger: Pioneer of Film Animation and her fantasy/horror novel Iron Impetigo. She hosts the Toon-In Talk Podcast and is pursuing a gemology degree at GIA. She’s currently working on a book about videogame movies, animator Tissa David, and a sequel to Iron Impetigo.

screenings.title: Trains, Children & Dreams: A Shorts Program
screenings.description: “The train that begins Bruce Conner’s Valse Triste also sets in motion a child’s dreaming. Like Conner’s synechdocal found footage classic A Movie, the loosely connected scenes that follow are retrieved from film history, as if to say that our dreams are made of movies, or vice versa. Wasn’t it a kind of dream to imagine, in 1896, that the Lumières’ train would tumble into the audience? Or that, in Ignacio Agüero’s One Hundred Children Waiting for the Train, the children of Lo Hermida, a working class neighborhood on the outskirts of Santiago, might one day see themselves on a real cinema screen? Or, despite the protest made by one of Harun Farocki’s young daughters—‘I don’t want to hear or see any more trains!’—the locomotive that arrives just as she and her sister drift off to sleep?” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.title: The Immigrant
screenings.description: Marion Cotillard has one of her greatest roles as Ewa, a Polish Catholic immigrant newly arrived in Ellis Island, trying to find the means to free her sister from quarantine in a c. 1921 New York City that’s full of lures and snares, among them Joaquin Phoenix’s smalltime pimp and tinhorn impresario and Jeremy Renner’s Bowery illusionist. A richly textured film of disarming depths of feeling from Gray, whose beguiling closing shot resonates long after the credits roll. “We effectively destroyed the film negative with various techniques,” said Darius Khondji, “to achieve the desired emotional aesthetic of that era.”

screenings.title: In the Mouth of Madness
screenings.description: Dir. John Carpenter. 1994, 95 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Sam Neill, Jürgen Prochnow, Julie Carmen, David Warner, John Glover, Charlton Heston. John Carpenter’s metacinematic tribute to the nightmarish underworlds of H. P. Lovecraft stars Sam Neill as a John Trent, a mild-mannered insurance investigator who gradually descends into hysteria while seeking the whereabouts Sutter Cane, a Lovecraft-esque cult writer who has gone missing. Upon arriving in a small New England town, Trent begins to realize that he may be caught within one of Cane’s stories, which only grows more nightmarish and sinister as he encounters surreal phenomena. The practical creature effects recall Lovecraft’s imagery while maintaining a sense of sly Carpenter humor that skirts the absurd. Aptly, a significant cult following has grown around In the Mouth of Madness in the decades since its release, and Neill’s unfettered portrayal of insanity has much to do with its beloved horror status. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: The Illiac Passion
screenings.description: Markopoulos corralled together the underground’s haute monde—Taylor Mead, Gerard Malanga, Jack Smith, Gregory Battcock and, in the role of Poseidon, Andy Warhol—for his radical reinterpretation of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound, in which the filmmaker can be heard on the soundtrack reciting Thoreau’s translation of the source text betwixt snatches of Bartók’s Cantata Profana. A rebel posing a direct challenge to Zeus’s absolute authority, Prometheus was a figure of fascination for Markopoulos, who saw in the outlaw Titan something of a kindred spirit. Hence his vainglorious description of The Illiac Passion: “Metamorphosis of the filmmaker. Passions of the filmmaker. Out of his breast the free flowing blood of the creation of a motion picture which depicts the passions of mankind and of everyman in general.”

screenings.title: Earth
screenings.description: Dovzhenko’s final silent feature, which depicts a clash between reactionary landowning peasants and modernizing paupers bringing the first tractor to their corner of the Ukrainian countryside, has by now spawned nearly a century of debate: is it a propagandist paean to the collectivization project in Stalin’s first Five-Year Plan, which would have catastrophic results in the Ukrainian Famine of 1932-33, or, as certain Soviet censors suspected, an on-the-sly celebration of a Ukrainian folk culture grounded in an ancient connection between the peasants and the soil they’ve so long tilled, threatened with impending erasure? What is not up for question is that Earth is among the greatest of films from the silent film canon, its distinct synthesis of Eisenstein, Pudovkin, and Vertov making it something like a summation of what had come before it, while its lyric ode to the natural world and those that live with it in harmony blazes a trail for the Ukrainian Poetic Cinema of the future to follow.

screenings.title: The Downtown Fest: The Mayflower + Q&A
The Enchanted Desna
screenings.description: The third film made by Solntseva from a script by her late husband and creative collaborator, The Enchanted Desna—an intimate epic in the magic-realist vein filmed on 70mm Sovscope and boasting state-of-the-art stereophonic sound—draws on Dovzhenko’s memories of his childhood on the banks of the Desna River in Chernihiv Oblast, moving freely between pre-revolutionary bucolic idyll, the horrors of World War II, and contemporary-set scenes. Winner of a Special Jury Prize at the San Sebastián Film Festival, Jean-Luc Godard’s favorite film of 1965 and, per critic Jonathan Rosenbaum, “among the most ravishingly beautiful and poetic spectacles ever made.”

screenings.title: High and Low
screenings.description: Kurosawa’s formal genius and rare humanism are on full display in this white-knuckle thriller—source of an upcoming remake by Spike Lee—which transposes the materials of an Ed McBain novel to contemporary Japan, starring Toshiro Mifune as a rich industrialist thrown into a nerve-shredding situation after, first believing his son has been kidnapped, discovering that his chauffeur’s child was taken by accident. Boasting nigh-constant visual invention, geometric precision of framing, an inventive narrative structure, and a bevy of staggering set pieces—the train hand-off! the down-and-dirty G.I. bar!—High & Low is a virtuoso work that’s also a deeply moral one, exploring the meaning of “justice” in a society defined by vast economic disparity.

screenings.description: One breathtaking composition follows another in Scorsese’s adaptation of Edith Wharton’s Pulitzer Prize–winning masterpiece about social mores (and taboos) amongst New York’s viperous moneyed classes in late 19th-century New York, brought to life by an all-star lineup of craftspeople including cinematographer Michael Ballhaus, editor Thelma Schoonmaker, production designer Dante Ferretti, and composer Elmer Bernstein. It was, Ryder stated during a recent appearance on (of all things) Hot Ones, “The role of a lifetime.”

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in China
screenings.description: No one wields a ’Scope frame with quite the same flexibility and dynamism as Hark, and the spectacular, Sergio Leone–inspired Once Upon a Time in China—perhaps the crucial film of the 1990s wuxia revival—shows Hark at his most flamboyant, keeping up with the human whirlwind that is Jet Li, here in the role of physician, martial artist, and 19th-century Cantonese folk hero Wong Fei-hung, who’s pitted against unscrupulous gangsters, human traffickers from the West, and his inconvenient feelings for “13th Aunt” Rosamund Kwan. Showstopping set pieces come fast and furious en route to a shoot-the-works shipboard finale; a monumental work of kinetic cinema.

screenings.title: Southland Tales (with J. Hoberman)
screenings.description: Dir. Richard Kelly. 2006, 145 mins. 35mm. With Dwayne Johnson, Seann William Scott, Sarah Michelle Gellar, Mandy Moore, Justin Timberlake, Miranda Richardson. In 2006, J. Hoberman called Southland Tales “a visionary film about the end of times. There hasn’t been anything comparable in American movies since Mulholland Drive.” Manic, messy, and endlessly referential, Southland Tales skewers George W. Bush, reality TV, and digital media to present an unforgettable satire of post-9/11 America. The film was not—and still may not be for everyone—but what it lacks in precision it more than makes up for in ambition. The film is set in the aftermath of two catastrophic nuclear attacks in Texas and follows the intertwining storylines of an action film actor, a porn star, and a pair of twin brothers. Stylistically it is no less convoluted, mashing up high and low art in a pitch-black comedy pastiche. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Antigone
screenings.description: Brecht’s adaptation of Sophocles’s Antigone—concerning the title character’s rebellion against the uncle, King Creon, who has condemned her to death—is performed in its entirety in Straub and Huillet’s final film set in the ancient world, which recalls their 1975 Moses und Aron in its antiquarian setting: the ruins of a Greek theatre in Segesta, Sicily.

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in China II
screenings.description: No one wields a ’Scope frame with quite the same flexibility and dynamism as Hark, and the spectacular, Sergio Leone–inspired Once Upon a Time in China II shows Hark at his most inspired, keeping up with the human whirlwind that is Jet Li, here returning to the role of physician, martial artist, and 19th-century Cantonese folk hero Wong Fei-hung. Traveling to Canton for a medical conference, Wong finds a city in chaos, with the anti-western White Lotus Cult seeking to snuff out foreign influence by any means necessary, and government forces—including officer Donnie Yen—resorting to violent measures against Dr. Sun Yat-sen’s republican revolutionaries. Unrelenting, utterly dazzling, pedal-to-the-metal action cinema.

screenings.title: Peeping Tom (with J. Hoberman)
screenings.description: Dir. Michael Powell. 1960, 101 mins. 4K DCP. With Karlheinz Böhm, Anna Massey, Moira Shearer. J. Hoberman writes,” A great film maudit can derail or even terminate a career. Michael Powell never recovered from the scandal of Peeping Tom.” Initially reviled, but now considered a classic study of cinematic voyeurism, Powell’s 1960 masterpiece concerns a young photographer obsessed with killing women and filming their final contorted expressions. Martin Scorsese has described it is a film that “says everything that can be said about filmmaking, [and] the process of dealing with film.” Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in China III
screenings.description: In Jet Li’s third outing as the legendary Wong Fei-hung, master of both inflicting pain and relieving it, Wong and Rosamund Kwan’s “13th Aunt” travel from Foshan to Beijing to meet with his father, there finding preparations underway for a colorful competition to crown a “Lion Dance King” and learning of a plot to assassinate statesman and court favorite Li Hongzhang. With leadership at home slipping into self-involved venality and foreign powers licking their chops at the prospect of dividing China up amongst themselves, Wong will have to hold the line one more time—and as one has come to expect of the series, the results are nothing short of spectacular.

screenings.title: Arsenal
screenings.description: The film that made Dovzhenko’s international reputation, Arsenal depicts—in thrillingly innovative, lyric cinematic language—a 1918 episode in the Russian Civil War, a worker’s uprising at Kyiv’s Arsenal Factory, and its brutal military suppression, in the midst of fighting between Bolshevik forces and the Central Rada of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, in whose ranks Dovzhenko may have served for a time. One of a quartet of films commissioned by Soviet authorities to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the October Revolution and, of the four, the most ambivalent, showing an understanding, in turns, of both the universalist, workers-of-the-world-unite Bolshevik cause and a Ukrainian nationalism rooted in soul and soil.

screenings.title: The Downtown Festival: Sitting Ducks + Q&A
Shchors
screenings.description: A biopic of the “Red Commander of the Ukraine,” Bolshevik commander Mykola Shchors, starring Yevgeny Samoylov in the title role, Shchors was personally commissioned by Joseph Stalin himself, and its production was a fraught one for Dovzhenko, whose health suffered grievously from the make-or-break pressure he faced to toe the line. The eventual results pleased the General Secretary—Dovzhenko would be awarded his first of two Stalin Prizes in 1941—though the film endures less for its vigorous, saber-rattling hagiography than the moments of ineffable poetry with which it’s embroidered, rooted as always in a deep sense of Ukrainian cultural tradition and relish in the natural world. “As in all [Dovzhenko’s] best work, Shchors leaves in the memory burning images of death and of passionate life” —Jay Leyda

screenings.title: The Downtown Festival: The Joyless Economy + Q&A
screenings.description: ABOUT THE DOWNTOWN FESTIVAL: The Downtown Festival is a multidisciplinary celebration of independent film, music, art, and culture held across Lower Manhattan each October. Founded and directed by filmmaker Rebekah Sherman-Myntti, the festival brings together artists across disciplines and generations through film premieres, anniversary screenings, live music performances, artist talks, and special one-night-only events. Programming is led by Sherman-Myntti and Associate Director Briana Bursten, with a focus on discovery, experimentation, community, and genuine artist-to-artist exchange. The festival’s film program runs October 9-18 at Roxy Cinema, with additional programming and special events taking place all over downtown.

screenings.title: The Terminator
screenings.description: Too many sequels and an incalculable cultural impact later, it’s sometimes forgotten what a hot and nasty little movie Cameron’s original Terminator was, dropping peak-physique Schwarzenegger into a sleazy Los Angeles of leather bars, punk rockers, and skid rows, where he quickly proceeds to killing cops by the score and tracking down mother-to-be of humankind’s savior Linda Hamilton. Working for the very last time with budget constraints, Cameron—and FX gurus Stan Winston and Gene Warren Jr.—deliver the goods and how, in a grimy lil’ chef d’oeuvre that gave us Cyberdine, Skynet, and a whole lexicon for discussing extinction-level singularity events.

screenings.title: Zvenygora
screenings.description: A hunt for the Scythian treasure trove of the title, a staple of Ukrainian folklore, becomes a jumping off point for a dizzying tour of a nation’s history, traditions, and fables, fleetly flitting between paeans to nature and man-made industry, a modern present and a mythic past, materialist fact and mystical fantasy. “My most interesting picture for me. I made it in one breath—a hundred days. Unusually complicated in structure, eclectic in form, the film gave me, a self-taught production worker, the fortuitous opportunity of trying myself out in every genre. It was a catalogue of all my creative abilities.” —Oleksandr Dovzhenko

screenings.title: Fantasia
screenings.description: Walt Disney (and eleven uncredited directors). 1940, 124 mins. U.S. DCP. Disney put it all on the line for this passion project combining his love of cartoons and classical music. Though the result baffled many in its day, Fantasia went on to be one of the most beloved, influential films of all time. Set to works by Bach, Tchaikovsky, Beethoven, Stravinsky, and more, the wordless, exquisitely hand-drawn segments that make up this ambitious masterpiece constitute a high point in animation. Among the most marvelous sequences is its finale, a diptych of the profane and the sacred juxtaposing Modest Mussorgsky’s frenetic and terrifying “Night on Bald Mountain” and Franz Schubert’s ecstatic hymn “Ave Maria.” The former, set on the diabolical Walpurgis Night, is perhaps cinema’s greatest Halloween party. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Purchase tickets for October 17 at 1:00 p.m. Purchase tickets for October 18 at 12:30 p.m. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Aerograd
screenings.description: Set in the Soviet Far East in the not-too-distant future, Dovzhenko’s film takes its title from a fictitious Siberian city that, as home to a strategically vital airfield, is targeted for conquest by the duplicitous forces of the Japanese Empire. A vision of technological utopianism and natural splendor, composed with dash and dynamism by cinematographer Eduard Tissé—a regular Eisenstein collaborator—in which the forces of the Revolution must contend with samurai saboteurs, counterrevolutionary kulaks, and rabble-rousing “Old Believer” Christians, pushing Soviet civilization into the wilds of the Pacific coast. Part spy thriller, part full-throated agitprop, part pantheistic bliss-out, and pure Dovzhenko.

screenings.title: Ivan
screenings.description: In making his first sound film, Dovzhenko proved himself every bit as much an innovator in the realm of the aural as he had been in that of the visual, creating a rich sonic tapestry in this melic ode to the construction of the Dnipro Hydroelectric Station and the men and women conscripted into its accomplishment, among them the eponymous Ukrainian villager. (Some critics, however, observed that Dovzhenko took a little too much pleasure in the doings of Ivan’s antagonist, a layabout kulak who refuses to bust his hump slaving away for the glory of the state.) As influential, arguably, as Earth before it, on the Ukrainian poetic cinema of the 1960s, and an achievement of towering stature.

screenings.title: Poem of the Sea
screenings.description: Based on a script left behind by Dovzhenko at his death, Poem of the Sea was finally filmed by his widow, Solntseva, a formidable filmmaker in her own right, her stated intention to work wholly “in accordance with Dovzhenko’s artistic conception, putting aside every trace of my own individual vision.” A companion piece of sorts to Ivan, likewise dealing with the construction of a dam and its impact on the surrounding countryside—in particular one soon-to-be-submerged village, birthplace of one General Fedorchenko (Boris Livanov), whose arrival for a visit in its final days stirs long-dormant memories. The feat of civil engineering documented here is the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant, opened in 1956 and destroyed by Russian forces in 2023, with catastrophic ecological results.

screenings.title: Prison + Who Are You Dorothy Dean? Book Launch and Q&A
screenings.description: Éditions 1989 celebrates the launch of the second edition of Who Are You Dorothy Dean?, the first book devoted to the late African American writer and actress. When Dorothy Dean (1932–1987) entered the 1960s New York underground scene, she quickly became one of its key figures—starring in six of Andy Warhol’s films and inspiring the likes of Robert Mapplethorpe and Robert Creeley.

screenings.title: The Red Violin + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: Following the success of 1993’s Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould, director François Girard and co-writer Don McKellar reunited to tell the story of The Red Violin, tracing the titular instrument’s journey from its creation in 17th-century Italy to an auction in 1990s Montreal–and the various musicians and owners it bewitches along the way. Girard mounts a handsome production with location shooting across five countries, from China to Austria, and Samuel L. Jackson shines as Charles Morritz, a fussy instrument appraiser who falls under the violin’s spell while decoding its secrets. Composer John Corigliano won the Academy Award for Best Original Score, and violinist Joshua Bell performed all of the solos in the film.

screenings.title: Nosferatu + Live Score
screenings.description: Nosferatu + Live Score by the Andrew Alden Ensemble The vampire film that started them all gets its shadow back. The Andrew Alden Ensemble performs an original score live beneath F.W. Murnau’s 1922 landmark — the New York chamber group whose violin, cello, keys, drums, and voice sit somewhere between contemporary classical and rock, writing music built for the room rather than the recording booth: immediate, physical, and made for this film alone. On screen, Count Orlok (Max Schreck) uncoils out of the Carpathians — all talons and teeth and rat-borne plague — and crosses the sea toward a town that cannot wake from him. A hundred years later the images still crawl.

screenings.title: Vampyr + Live Score
screenings.description: Carl Theodor Dreyer’s 1932 fever dream is less a horror film than a nightmare filmed at the moment of waking — fog, drifting shadows, a scythe, a burial seen from inside the coffin. The Andrew Alden Ensemble scores it live with violin, electric guitar, piano, synthesizers, and percussion, the New York group’s music moving with the film’s logic of dread rather than against it. A young traveler, Allan Gray (Julian West), arrives in a riverside village held under the spell of a vampire, and the world begins to come loose at the edges. Dreyer made it as sound cinema was being born and produced something stranger than either silence or speech; performed with a live original score, it turns stranger still.

screenings.title: The Draughtsman's Contract + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: Set in a richly exaggerated 17th-century England, Peter Greenaway’s sumptuous and sensuously charged brainteaser catapulted him to the forefront of international art cinema. Adorned with intricate wordplay, extravagant costumes and opulent photography, Greenaway’s first narrative feature weaves a labyrinthine mystery around the maxim “draw what you see, not what you know.” An aristocratic wife (Janet Suzman) commissions a young, cocksure draughtsman (Anthony Higgins) to sketch her husband’s property while he is away—in exchange for a fee, room and board, and one sexual favor for each of the twelve drawings. As the draughtsman becomes more entrenched in the devious schemings in this seemingly idyllic country home, curious details emerge in his drawings that may reveal a murder.
screenings.country: Instruments of Desire Comedy, Drama, Mystery

screenings.title: Tár + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: From writer-producer-director Todd Field comes TÁR, starring Cate Blanchett as Lydia Tár, the celebrated chief conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic. We meet Tár at the height of her career, as she’s preparing both a book launch and a much-anticipated live recording of Mahler’s Fifth Symphony. Over the ensuing weeks, her life and career unravel as allegations of misconduct erode her carefully cultivated public image. The result is a searing examination of artistic authority, institutional politics, and the blurred boundary between mentorship and exploitation.
